assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned superconducting circuits into controllable artificial atoms strongly coupled to single microwave photons, giving dispersive readout, qubit-qubit coupling via resonators and the architecture used by essentially every superconducting processor. The idea is original, clear, and its impact on quantum technology and microwave quantum optics is large and demonstrably lasting. I work in this area, so I judge it from inside the field.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) split between theory and experiment. A fair trio is Schoelkopf (experiment and subsequent development), Wallraff (first strong-coupling demonstration) and Blais (theory); Girvin has an equally strong claim to the theory side and would be the hardest omission. Credit for the Yale group is shared among several people not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: two decades of independent replication across many labs, and the physics is stable. Timing is the question: the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, so an immediate second prize in the same family needs justification as a distinct discovery.
uncertainties: Disclosure: Chalmers colleagues (Delsing, Wilson) and my own circuit-QED theory work are close to this topic, so I discount my own enthusiasm.
Proximity to the 2025 prize could be viewed as too soon.
Allocation between Girvin and Blais for the theory share is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire flat-band physics, with correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable carbon system. It created a major new field combining a clear theoretical prediction with a striking experiment; originality and breadth of impact are high.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction (2011) and the Jarillo-Herrero group experiments (2018) are the decisive pair. Credit to Cao, Fatemi and others in the experiment, and to Pablo's group generally, is a possible complication, but the three names support a clean configuration of one theory pair plus one experimentalist.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced independently in many groups and extended to other moire systems, though the nature of the superconductivity remains under debate; the discovery itself is secure and timely.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism in the superconducting phase is unresolved.
Allocation to individual early-career experimentalists is not captured by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault tolerance establish that large quantum computations are possible despite noise, and topological codes underlie today's hardware roadmaps. This is foundational, and as a quantum-computing theorist I regard error correction as the requirement for broad use of processors.
assessment.attribution: Shor's code and fault-tolerance contributions and Kitaev's topological code and anyon-based ideas are decisive; Steane's independent code is also important, so the three-name set is defensible, but I propose the two with the broadest foundational reach. Others (Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov, Ben-Or) are not on the credited list, so attribution is partly unfairly narrow.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of below-threshold logical qubits are recent and still developing, so the confirmation is strong on theory but young in hardware; recognition is arguably timely or slightly early.
uncertainties: Whether this is physics rather than computer science for the Nobel statutes.
Credit is spread over many contributors beyond three.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped-ion quantum computation and simulation started from the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal and led to the highest-fidelity entangling gates and programmable quantum simulators. Strong physical clarity and lasting impact on quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the scheme and Blatt realised key entangling operations and scaled it; David Wineland already received the 2012 prize for ion control, and credit for experiments by Monroe, Wineland's group and others is not on the list, so allocation is incomplete but the proposed trio is coherent.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of independent confirmation, though part of the field's recognition was partly addressed by 2012.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with other candidates that include Cirac and Zoller.
Experimental credit to Monroe and others is not available.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson was made possible by the conception and construction of ATLAS and CMS, a landmark of experimental physics confirming the mechanism of mass generation after the 2013 theory prize.
assessment.attribution: Instrument leadership is a natural basis for recognition, with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as founding spokespersons or project leaders; however, the discovery came from collaborations of thousands, and the Nobel statute difficulty of crediting a few people is acute.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed and over a decade old; recognition is arguably overdue, though the choice of individuals is contentious.
uncertainties: Fair attribution among collaboration leaders, accelerator builders and analysis leads is unresolved.
The 2013 prize already recognised the theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models, the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site microscopy, transforming how strongly correlated matter is studied.
assessment.attribution: Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger provided decisive experimental realisations; Cirac and Zoller proposed the theory and Greiner's Mott-insulator work with Bloch and Hansch is central. The five-name list is too large, and omitting Zoller may seem unfair given Jaksch et al., who are not listed.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and repeatedly confirmed, with growing use in quantum simulators; timeliness is good.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with Cirac and Zoller that appear in other candidates.
The line between discovery and a tool is blurry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84, E91) showed that quantum mechanics can secure communication, founding quantum cryptography and a major part of quantum information science.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) are the clear originators; Ekert's entanglement-based protocol is independent. The list holds two spellings of Ekert, so I use the exact string 'Artur K. Ekert' as one person.
assessment.maturity: Foundational and widely demonstrated in the lab and in commercial and satellite systems; broad confirmation, though real-world security remains an engineering concern.
uncertainties: Duplicate credited spellings for Ekert make the credit list ambiguous.
Weight between physics foundations and communications engineering.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, and the experimental demonstration in HgTe, created a central field of topological quantum matter, with a clear mechanism and large conceptual impact.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the key theoretical prediction, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposed HgTe and Molenkamp's group observed edge transport; Hasan's role centres on three-dimensional materials. The three-name configuration is plausible but excludes the HgTe proposers.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many groups, over fifteen years old, so timely.
uncertainties: Attribution between the 2D and 3D topological insulator discoveries is disputed.
The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is not in the credited names.
